title: GPT-2, explained: no fine-tuning, just a prompt—and the model learns tasks on its own
summary: GPT-2 scales GPT-1 up to 1.5 billion parameters and retrains it on 40 GB of web text, then drops fine-tuning entirely: write the task as a prompt and the model does reading comprehension, summarization, translation, and QA zero-shot. We unpack the core idea that “a task is also text,” WebText and byte-level BPE, how prompts were phrased for each task, the results, and then how the paper checks for memorization—and where it got its parameter counts wrong.
ai_summary: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (OpenAI, 2019) argues that language models trained on large and diverse enough text will learn many tasks without explicit supervision. The authors built 40 GB of WebText from upvoted Reddit outbound links and trained GPT-2, up to 1.5 billion parameters, keeping GPT-1's architecture but moving to pre-layer normalization, byte-level BPE, and a 1024-token context. With no fine-tuning, only prompts, GPT-2 set zero-shot records on 7 of 8 language modeling datasets and reached 55 F1 on CoQA reading comprehension, while summarization, translation, and QA remained rudimentary. Every task improved with model size, and even the largest model still underfit WebText.
brief: Problem: every task needs its own labeled dataset, so multitask learning doesn't scale. Can a model learn tasks from natural language itself?
Method: train a Transformer decoder with up to 1.5B parameters on 40 GB of WebText; with no fine-tuning, write the task as a prompt and let the model continue.
Results: zero-shot records on 7 of 8 language modeling datasets; 55 F1 on CoQA; summarization, translation, and QA are still rudimentary but all improve steadily with scale.
Limits: zero-shot is far from practical, and the paper's reported parameter counts are wrong; GPT-3 later makes this path work with few-shot prompts and much larger scale.

paper.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
paper.authors: Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever

cover.headline: A close read of the GPT-2 paper

big.label: GPT-2 is over an order of magnitude larger than GPT-1

sections.h: Start with the conclusion: what the paper actually did

blocks.p: In February 2019, OpenAI's Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei, and Ilya Sutskever released this paper. Like the earlier GPT-1 paper, it did not go on arXiv; it was a PDF on OpenAI's website. The largest model in the paper is **GPT-2**, with 1.5 billion parameters—more than an order of magnitude larger than GPT-1.

Its central claim is right in the title: **language models are unsupervised multitask learners**. Train a model to guess the next word on large and diverse enough text, and it **learns many tasks by itself**—reading comprehension, summarization, translation, QA—with no fine-tuning and no changes to its architecture. You just write the task as a piece of text and let the model continue. This is called **zero-shot**.

To do this, the authors crawled more than 8 million web pages from upvoted Reddit links—40 GB of text total—and called the dataset WebText. The result: GPT-2 set zero-shot records on 7 of 8 language modeling datasets. Given a passage and a conversation history, it reached 55 F1 on CoQA reading comprehension, matching or beating 3 of 4 supervised baselines that used more than 127,000 human-labeled question-answer pairs. On summarization, translation, and QA it was still far from practical, but every one of those tasks improved steadily as models got larger.

This paper is the bridge in the series. GPT-1 showed that pretraining plus fine-tuning works and hinted at zero-shot at the end; GPT-2 turns that hint into the main event, **making “no fine-tuning, just prompts” a serious research direction for the first time**; a year later GPT-3 scales up by more than 100× and uses few-shot prompts to make the approach genuinely useful.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: GPT-2 = GPT-1's architecture, lightly modified + scaled to 1.5 billion parameters + trained on 40 GB of high-quality web text. With no fine-tuning, just prefix the task in text (for example, add “TL;DR:” after an article to get a summary), and the model can do reading comprehension, summarization, translation, and QA. Performance rises steadily with model size, and even the largest model still underfits.

callout.title: Three small concepts you need for this paper
callout.text: Don't worry if you haven't met them; these three are enough:
list: **GPT-1**: a Transformer decoder pretrained on books and then fine-tuned for specific tasks. See the previous article in this series, “GPT-1.”
**Zero-shot**: the model sees no training examples for the task and updates no parameters; it simply takes the test.
**Perplexity (PPL)**: how “surprised” a language model is by text. A perplexity of 10 is loosely like choosing among 10 words at every step; lower is better.

sections.h: Problem: every task needs its own labeled data—and that doesn't scale

blocks.p: The paper's opening judgment is blunt: machine learning systems of the time were “narrow experts,” not “competent generalists.” The standard approach was to collect examples of the desired behavior for each task, train a model to imitate them, then evaluate it on held-out examples from the same distribution. Such systems are fragile to small changes in data distribution or task description.

Multitask learning is a way out, but the authors do the math: from a meta-learning perspective, each (dataset, objective) pair is effectively one training example. The largest multitask efforts at the time used only 10 and 17 such pairs, while existing learning methods usually need hundreds or thousands of examples to learn something generalizable. Manually piling up datasets and designing objectives is unlikely to reach the required scale.
So the paper tries something else: **can a model learn tasks from natural language itself, without a human telling it which part is the input and which part is the answer?**

sections.h: Core idea: a task can itself be written as text

blocks.p: The paper first expresses “doing a task” in probability: learning a task means estimating the conditional distribution p(output | input). But a general system may need to do different tasks for the same input, so it should estimate **p(output | input, task)**—it needs to know, besides the input, what to do.

Previously, “what to do” was communicated through model architecture—a task-specific encoder or decoder—or through the training algorithm. The paper points out that **language itself can flexibly describe the task, the input, and the output**. A translation example can be written as one string: (translate to French, English text, French text); a reading comprehension example can be written as (answer the question, document, question, answer).

parts.desc: A sequence of text made up of tokens s_{1}, …, s_{n}
The probability of the next token s_{i}, given all previous tokens. That is what a language model learns.
The probability of the whole text is the product of these per-step probabilities. It lets the model both score any text and generate it one token at a time.

formula.note: The key point: if the task, input, and answer all live in the same text, then “predict the answer” is just part of “predict the next word.” As the paper puts it, the supervised objective is the same as the unsupervised objective, only evaluated on a subset of the sequence—so the global optimum of the unsupervised objective is also the global optimum of the supervised objective.

callout.title: The web is full of “natural demonstrations”
callout.text: The paper finds many naturally occurring translation demonstrations in WebText, such as “as they say in French: Je ne suis pas un imbecile [I'm not a fool],” or an English news story that quotes French and then gives an English translation. A model trying to predict the next word accurately, if it is large enough, would pick up that when French is followed by something like “which means,” an English translation should come next. The authors' conjecture: with enough capacity, a language model will infer and execute the tasks shown in text, simply to predict that text better.

blocks.p: The paper admits this only holds in theory. The real question is whether, in practice, the unsupervised objective can be optimized well enough. Preliminary experiments show that large enough language models can indeed learn multitask in this setting—just much more slowly than with explicit supervision.

sections.h: Data: WebText, with humans filtering first

blocks.p: To expose the model to as many task demonstrations as possible, the data has to be **large and diverse**. Earlier language models were mostly trained on a single domain: news, Wikipedia, or fiction. Web-crawl data such as Common Crawl is far larger but much messier; one study found that many documents were “mostly unintelligible.”

The authors' compromise: only crawl pages **already filtered by humans**. They scraped all outbound links on Reddit that received at least 3 karma (upvotes), treating it as a rough signal that someone found the link interesting, useful, or funny.

blocks.p: **Input representation**: to let the model score **any string**, GPT-2 switches to **byte-level BPE**. Standard BPE operates on Unicode characters; to cover all Unicode characters, the base vocabulary would exceed 130,000. Byte-level BPE needs a base vocabulary of only 256 bytes. But applying BPE directly to bytes produces many redundant tokens such as dog, dog., dog!, dog?, wasting vocabulary slots. To avoid this, the paper prevents BPE from merging across character categories—letters, punctuation, and so on—except for spaces. The final vocabulary has 50,257 tokens.

The advantage: the model can be evaluated on any language modeling dataset, regardless of preprocessing, tokenization, or vocabulary size. The <UNK> token, extremely rare in WebText, appears only 26 times in 40 billion bytes.

sections.h: Model: GPT-1's architecture, in four sizes

blocks.p: The model largely follows GPT-1, with a few changes:

list: **Layer normalization moved to the input of each sub-block** (like a pre-activation residual network), with an extra layer norm added after the final self-attention block. This “pre-norm” layout later became standard for large models because it makes very deep networks easier to train.

**Residual-layer initialization scaled by depth**: initial weights are multiplied by 1/√N, where N is the number of residual layers. More layers means more values accumulate on the residual path; scaling them down keeps the signal from growing too large.
**Vocabulary expanded to 50,257**; **context size increased from 512 to 1024 tokens**; batch size increased to 512.

blocks.p: The paper trained four models with roughly log-uniform sizes. The smallest is equivalent to the original GPT; the second-smallest is equivalent to the largest BERT; the largest is GPT-2. The learning rate for each model was manually tuned for the best perplexity on a 5% held-out sample of WebText.

fig.title: The four models: the paper's parameter counts don't match what the architecture implies
fig.subtitle: “Estimated from architecture” is our calculation: about 12 × d_{model}^{2} per layer, plus 50,257 × d_{model} for vocabulary and 1024 × d_{model} for position, ignoring small terms such as layer norm. Amber marks GPT-2
fig.note: Every model comes out larger when counted from its architecture than the paper says. The smallest model's 117M is close to the ≈116M you get from GPT-1's configuration (40,000-token vocab, 512 context), so the paper seems to have reused GPT-1's figure without adding the larger vocabulary and longer context. OpenAI later admitted in the open-source code notes that the original parameter counts were wrong and updated them to 124M, 355M, 774M, and 1.5B, consistent with the estimates here.

blocks.p: The paper also makes a point: **all models still underfit WebText**. With more training time, held-out perplexity kept improving. In Figure 4, train and test perplexity are nearly identical and both fall as models get larger—so even GPT-2 is far from “memorizing” the training data.

quiz.q: Why does GPT-2 use byte-level BPE instead of BPE over Unicode characters?
options: It's faster at the byte level
Unicode has too many characters, so the base vocabulary would exceed 130,000; bytes only number 256 and can represent any string
To make the model learn only English
quiz.why: The point is to let the model compute probabilities for arbitrary text. Byte-level BPE has a base vocabulary of just 256, so there are no out-of-vocabulary cases; merges then learn common subword pieces. The paper adds a rule to avoid merging dog with its following punctuation into many redundant tokens.

sections.h: How to make it do tasks without fine-tuning: write the task as a prompt

blocks.p: All results are zero-shot: no parameters are updated. You arrange the context the model sees, then let it generate or score the continuation. Different tasks use different phrasings:

callout.title: TL;DR is the web's “natural prompt”
callout.text: TL;DR stands for “Too Long; Didn't Read.” People on the web often put it at the end of a long post, followed by a sentence or two of summary. The model saw this pattern countless times in WebText, so when it sees “TL;DR:” it knows to write a summary. The paper ran a control: removing the TL;DR prompt lowered the overall summarization score by 6.4 points, showing that natural language alone can trigger a specific behavior. It is one of the earliest glimpses of today's prompt engineering.

quiz.q: The paper says removing the “TL;DR:” prompt lowers the summarization score by 6.4 points. What does that show?
options: TL;DR is a special control symbol
The model learned from training data that TL;DR is usually followed by a summary, so natural language alone can specify the task
quiz.why: To the model, TL;DR is just ordinary text, not a specially designed control. The model learned a pattern from the web: TL;DR is followed by a summary. That lets a prompt switch its behavior—exactly the evidence that language itself can specify a task.

sections.h: Result one: language modeling, records on 7 of 8 datasets

blocks.p: First, the thing a language model does by default: language modeling. Models trained on WebText were evaluated directly on other language modeling benchmarks, with no training or fine-tuning. Those datasets contain aggressively normalized text—split punctuation and contractions, shuffled sentences, even <UNK> tokens—so they are clearly out-of-distribution for GPT-2. Using invertible de-tokenizers to remove those artifacts improved GPT-2's perplexity by 2.5 to 5 points.

fig.title: Zero-shot language modeling: GPT-2 beats prior best everywhere except 1BW
fig.subtitle: From paper Table 3. PPL is perplexity (lower is better), ACC is accuracy %, and BPB / BPC are bits per byte / per character (lower is better). Blue marks GPT-2
fig.note: The gains are largest on small datasets such as Penn Treebank and WikiText-2, which have only one to two million training tokens. 1BW is the only dataset GPT-2 did not beat; the paper attributes this to 1BW being both the largest and sentence-shuffled, which destroys all long-range structure.

blocks.p: **LAMBADA** specifically tests long-range dependencies: the goal is to predict the last word of a sentence, and humans need at least 50 tokens of context to get it right. GPT-2 cut perplexity from 99.8 to 8.6 and lifted accuracy from 19% to 52.66%. After examining the errors, the paper found that most were fluent continuations that simply could not serve as the sentence's **final word**; adding a stop-word filter raised accuracy to 63.24%, 4 points above the previous best.
**Winograd commonsense reasoning**: GPT-2 scored 70.70%, 7 points above the previous best. But the paper cautions that this dataset has only 273 questions.

sections.h: Result two: zero-shot on tasks—some close, some still weak

fig.title: Zero-shot results on five tasks: reading comprehension close to supervised models; summarization and translation still rudimentary

blocks.p: **Reading comprehension** comes closest to being useful: given the passage, conversation history, and a final “A:”, GPT-2 with greedy decoding reaches 55 F1, while the supervised systems it is compared against trained on more than 127,000 human-labeled QA pairs. However, the paper's analysis found that it often uses simple retrieval-style heuristics—for example, when asked “who,” it picks a person's name from the passage.

**Summarization** looks like summarization but often only summarizes the end of the article or gets details wrong (such as how many cars were in a crash, or whether a logo was on a hat or a shirt). By ROUGE score, it is only slightly better than picking 3 random sentences.

**Translation** surprised the authors most: they had deliberately filtered non-English pages out of WebText, and after the fact a language detector found only about 10 MB of French—roughly 500 times smaller than the French monolingual corpora commonly used in earlier unsupervised translation research. Even so, GPT-2 scored 11.5 BLEU on French-to-English, beating several unsupervised translation baselines. English-to-French reached only 5 BLEU, because its French ability is far weaker than its English ability.

**Question answering** tests how much knowledge is stored in the model's parameters. GPT-2's exact match is only 4.1%, but the smallest model did not even beat the 1.0% baseline of answering with the most common answer per question type; GPT-2 answered correctly 5.3 times as often. Its confidence is also fairly reliable: on the 1% of questions it was most confident about, accuracy reached 63.1%.

He then added: actually only 14 were right, and the other 3 “should have been right,” but the questions leaked the answer.

blocks.p: All tasks share one pattern: **performance improves steadily with model size**. Figure 1 in the paper shows that zero-shot reading comprehension, translation, summarization, and QA all improve as parameter count grows; the abstract calls this “log-linear” improvement. This is the phenomenon GPT-3 and “Scaling Laws” later studied systematically.

With training data this large, could the test questions have appeared in the training data already? The paper ran a dedicated overlap analysis: it put every 8-gram (8 consecutive words) in the WebText training set into a Bloom filter, then checked how many 8-grams from each test set also appeared in the training data.

fig.title: Overlap with WebText is mostly no greater than overlap with a dataset's own training set
fig.subtitle: How many 8-grams in each test set also appear in training data, from paper Table 6. Amber marks 1BW
fig.note: Common language modeling test sets overlap with WebText by 1% to 6%, averaging 3.2%; their average overlap with their own training sets is 5.9%, even higher. 1BW's overlap with its own training set is close to 13.2%. The paper also found that a WikiText-103 test set article appeared in its own training set.

list: **LAMBADA**: average overlap 1.2%. Removing all overlapping samples and recalculating changes perplexity from 8.6 to 8.7 and drops accuracy from 63.2% to 62.9%—a small impact.

**CoQA**: about 15% of the news articles appear in WebText, and on those articles the model's F1 is about 3 points higher. Overall, overlap accounts for roughly 0.5 to 1.0 F1 improvement. CoQA was released after WebText's cutoff date, so the questions and answers themselves are not in the training data.
**Winograd**: only 10 questions have 8-gram overlap with WebText, and 2 of those are false positives.

blocks.p: The paper concludes that data overlap gives a **small but consistent** benefit, but for most datasets the overlap is no worse than the usual overlap between their own training and test sets. It suggests that n-gram overlap deduplication should become a standard check when building NLP datasets.

list: **The parameter counts are wrong**: Table 2's 117M, 345M, 762M, and 1542M are all smaller than what the architecture implies (see the estimation table above). The smallest model's 117M is close to the estimate from GPT-1's configuration, so it likely omits the larger vocabulary and longer context.

**Two ways of stating the data size**: Section 2.1 says WebText is 40 GB of text, and Section 3.1 says <UNK> appears 26 times in “40 billion bytes.” 40 GB is about 40 billion bytes, so the two statements agree; they are just different units. Don't read them as two datasets.

**The “7 out of 8” accounting**: Table 3 has 10 columns, but LAMBADA's perplexity and accuracy count as one dataset, and CBT's two question types count as one, so there are 8 datasets. GPT-2 only failed to beat the previous best on 1BW.

**The paper does not actually describe GPT-2's release**: because OpenAI worried about misuse (such as generating fake news at scale), it initially released only the smallest model, then released larger versions in stages over several months. The full 1.5-billion-parameter model was only released in November 2019. This staged-release decision was controversial at the time, but the paper itself does not discuss it.

blocks.p: The paper's discussion section is measured:

list: **Zero-shot is far from practical**: reading comprehension is competitive, but summarization is only “qualitatively similar” and still rudimentary by the metrics. The paper writes that, from a practical application standpoint, GPT-2's zero-shot performance is still nowhere near usable.

**Many tasks remain at chance level**: the authors acknowledge that on many practical tasks GPT-2 is surely no better than random guessing; even on QA and translation, it only begins to beat simple baselines when the model is large enough.

**The unidirectional limitation**: the paper notes that it is unclear whether more data and capacity for GPT-2 can compensate for the inefficiency of unidirectional representations, which BERT had already demonstrated. The authors plan to fine-tune GPT-2 on benchmarks such as GLUE to answer this.

blocks.p: **The story after.** The paper's conclusion says that large-capacity models trained on sufficiently large and diverse data will begin to learn many tasks without explicit supervision. A year later, GPT-3 (2020) pushed this to its extreme: 175 billion parameters, and **few-shot prompts** (a few examples in the context) instead of zero-shot, matching or even beating fine-tuned models on many tasks. That same year, “Scaling Laws” turned “bigger is better” into a predictable power law.

GPT-2 itself left several lasting influences: pre-layer normalization became a standard architecture for large models; byte-level BPE was adopted by many subsequent models; and the idea of “using a prompt to elicit a task” later grew into the entire field of prompt engineering.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: Why does the paper say the global optimum of the supervised objective is also the global optimum of the unsupervised objective?
options: Because both use the same optimizer
Because if the task, input, and answer are all written in the same text, predicting the answer is just part of predicting the next word
Because supervised data is a subset of unsupervised data
Because language models don't need labels
quiz.why: When the answer is part of the text, the supervised objective is just predicting the next word at the answer positions—a subset of the language modeling objective. The paper also cautions that this is only true in theory; whether the objective can be optimized well enough in practice is the real issue, and preliminary experiments show learning is much slower than with direct supervision.

quiz.q: Many of GPT-2's LAMBADA errors were fluent continuations but not the sentence's final word. How did the paper improve this?
options: Add a stop-word filter that approximates the constraint of having to be the sentence's final word
Only allow words that appear in the context
quiz.why: The paper added stop-word filtering, raising accuracy from 52.66% to 63.24%. The previous best method restricted output to words that appeared in the context; the paper found this actively hurts GPT-2, because 19% of answers are not in the context.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer the following:

list: What does p(output | input, task) mean? Why is language able to describe tasks?
How was WebText built? Why were Wikipedia documents removed?
What problem does byte-level BPE solve?
What three architectural changes does GPT-2 make to GPT-1?
For zero-shot summarization, translation, and reading comprehension, what does the model see?
Which tasks were close to practical? Which were still weak?
How did the paper check overlap between test data and training data, and what did it conclude?
Why don't the paper's reported parameter counts match the counts implied by the architecture?
